sections.h: Boasting in weakness (2 Corinthians 10 to 13)
sections.b: In 2 Corinthians 10 to 13 Paul rejects boasting in power, pedigree and visions, and boasts of weakness. His rule is Jeremiah's: "If anyone is to boast, let it be in this alone" (Jeremiah 9:24), and in his words, "Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord" (2 Corinthians 10:17). In what he calls the fool's speech he lists his Jewish credentials (11:22), a long catalog of beatings and shipwrecks (11:23-29), and an escape in a basket (11:32-33). He declines to rest his case on a vision of Paradise (12:1-6) and reports the Lord's word about the thorn: "Power is made complete in weakness" (12:9). The point for the Corinthians was that status and eloquence are not the proof of an apostle.

common: Paul's boasting is irony: a boast that mocks boasting.
uncommon: The fool's speech also makes a serious claim to apostolic credentials that the rivals could not match.

sections.h: The 'super-apostles' of 2 Corinthians 11 and 12
sections.b: Paul twice mocks a group as "super-apostles" (2 Corinthians 11:5; 12:11; Greek hyperlian apostoloi, "beyond the limit" apostles, a sarcastic coinage), and once calls some "false apostles" and "workers who cheat" (11:13). Views: they are the Jerusalem apostles (argued by some scholars); they are the same visiting teachers Paul calls false apostles, named ironically (many recent commentators); they are Judaizing Jewish-Christian missionaries (a common proposal), or Jews shaped by Hellenistic ideas (Georgi). Paul says they preach "another Jesus", boast of visions and Jewish credentials, carry recommendations and take pay. The evidence is mainly Paul's own replies.
sections.refs: 2 Corinthians 11:4-5; 2 Corinthians 11:12-15; 2 Corinthians 11:20-23; 2 Corinthians 12:11; Galatians 2:6-9; Revelation 2:2

sections.h: The thorn in the flesh (2 Corinthians 12:7)
sections.b: After telling of a vision of Paradise, Paul says that "a thorn was given to me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, to beat me" (2 Corinthians 12:7). He prayed three times for it to leave and was told, "My grace is enough for you. Power is made complete in weakness" (12:9). He does not say what it was. The main readings are a physical illness (eye trouble, malaria, migraine, epilepsy), human opponents (Chrysostom), temptation or spiritual struggle (Calvin; many medieval writers), emotional distress, or a demonic attack. The Septuagint uses "thorn" for hostile neighbors (Numbers 33:55; Ezekiel 28:24), and the Lord's answer treats the thorn as a means of grace.
sections.refs: 2 Corinthians 12:7-10; Galatians 4:13-15; Numbers 33:55; Ezekiel 28:24; Job 2:6; Mark 14:32-42

common: The thorn is unnamed, and the passage is about the answer rather than the identity.

sections.h: The third heaven and Paradise (2 Corinthians 12:2-4)
sections.b: Paul tells of "a man in Christ" who, fourteen years before, was "snatched up as far as the third heaven" and "into Paradise", where he heard words that cannot be spoken (2 Corinthians 12:2-4). Almost all scholars take the man to be Paul. Ancient Jewish writings count three, five, seven or ten heavens and sometimes put Paradise in the third (2 Enoch 8; Apocalypse of Moses 37:5). Later rabbinic and mystical writings tell of ascents (Hagigah 14b; the Hekhalot texts). These are comparisons, many of them later than Paul. Augustine read the third heaven as the highest kind of vision, and Aquinas taught that Paul saw the essence of God in the rapture; Gregory Palamas taught that he saw the uncreated light. Luke 23:43 and Revelation 2:7 use "Paradise" for the place of the righteous.
sections.refs: 2 Corinthians 12:1-6; Luke 23:43; Revelation 2:7; Genesis 2:8; 2 Enoch 8; Apocalypse of Moses 37:5; Hagigah 14b

sections.h: Paul answers his critics (2 Corinthians 10 to 13)
sections.b: In 2 Corinthians 10 to 13 Paul defends his authority against visiting rivals who called him weak in person, poor as a speaker and unwilling to take money like a real teacher. He claims his field (10:13), warns of a different Jesus (11:4), lists his credentials as a Jew (11:22) and his hardships (11:23-33), tells of a vision and a thorn (12:1-10), and says his third visit will not spare the unrepentant (13:2). He lived on his own labor and on gifts from other churches, never from Corinth (11:7-9; 12:13). Acts gives only part of the suffering he lists here.
sections.refs: 2 Corinthians 10:1-11; 2 Corinthians 11:5-33; 2 Corinthians 12:11-21; 2 Corinthians 13:1-10; Acts 14:19; Acts 16:22-24

sections.h: Satan in disguise and the messenger of Satan (2 Corinthians 11 and 12)
sections.b: Paul compares the Corinthians to Eve, fooled by the snake (2 Corinthians 11:3), and says that "Satan himself takes on the look of an angel of light" so that his servants can pass as servants of righteousness (11:14-15). The idea of Satan appearing as an angel to Eve appears in the Life of Adam and Eve, a Jewish retelling that was never part of any Bible's main canon; Paul may know a tradition like it. Later in the letter "a messenger of Satan" is allowed to beat Paul, as Satan is allowed to strike Job within God's limits (12:7; compare Job 2:6). Even Satan's attack serves a purpose Paul can name.
sections.refs: 2 Corinthians 11:3; 2 Corinthians 11:13-15; 2 Corinthians 12:7; Genesis 3:1-6; Job 2:6; Life of Adam and Eve 9:1

sections.h: The catalog of Paul's sufferings (2 Corinthians 11:23-33)
sections.b: Paul lists five synagogue lashings, three beatings with rods, a stoning, three shipwrecks, a night and a day at sea, constant travel and danger, hunger, cold and his worry for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:23-29). He ends with his flight from Damascus in a basket (11:32-33). Acts tells only some of this. The form follows Stoic lists of hardships, but Paul's purpose is the opposite of the philosophers': he lists them as weakness, in which Christ's power shows (12:9-10). Suffering is not good in itself, but the place where Paul is most like the crucified Christ (13:4).
sections.refs: 2 Corinthians 11:23-33; 2 Corinthians 12:9-10; 2 Corinthians 13:4; 2 Corinthians 4:7-12; Deuteronomy 25:3; Acts 14:19

sections.h: Signs of an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12)
sections.b: Paul says that "the signs that mark an apostle" were done among the Corinthians: signs, wonders and acts of power (2 Corinthians 12:12). He puts "complete endurance" first, since patient suffering is his main mark of an apostle, and he mocks rivals he calls "super-apostles" and "false apostles" (11:5, 13). The question of who counts as an apostle, and whether the signs continue, divides churches (see the card at 2 Corinthians 12:12).

sections.h: False apostles (2 Corinthians 11:13-15)
sections.b: Paul calls the rivals in Corinth "false apostles" who "disguising themselves as apostles of Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:13). Others were tested by churches by whether they preached the same Jesus (11:4), whether they took the church's money (11:20; compare Didache 11:3-6), and whether their lives showed the cross. The warning is general: servants of Satan can disguise themselves as servants of righteousness (11:15).

sections.h: Paul, Corinth and the money (2 Corinthians 11 and 12)
sections.b: Paul refused pay from Corinth, which the Corinthians took as a slight, because in a patronage culture the person who paid owned the teacher. He took support from Macedonian churches instead (2 Corinthians 11:7-9) and promised never to be a weight on the Corinthians (12:13-14). His rivals evidently took money and used their pedigrees (11:20-22). Some Corinthians suspected him of profiting from the collection through Titus (12:16-18). He planned a third visit, after a painful second one (12:14; 13:1).

sections.h: Not every prayer for healing is answered (2 Corinthians 12:7-9)
sections.b: Paul begged the Lord three times to remove the thorn and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:8-9). He does not say the thorn was an illness, but the case has long been used in discussions of healing. Churches answer in different ways, and the thorn is read as a trial that God used for a good end by Chrysostom and Calvin, among others. See the card at 2 Corinthians 12:7.

sections.h: Snatched up: the word behind 'rapture' (2 Corinthians 12:2-4)
sections.b: The Greek verb harpazō ("to snatch away") is used for Paul's own ascent to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2, 4) and for believers "caught up" to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). The Latin Bible has raptus and rapiemur, and English "rapture" comes from them. The same verb does not make these the same event: one is a private vision of one man, the other a gathering of the living at Christ's return.

sections.h: The closing blessing of 2 Corinthians (13:14)
sections.b: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you" (2 Corinthians 13:14) is the only blessing in Paul's letters that names Christ, God and the Spirit together. It is not a statement of doctrine, but it shows the three already in common worship. Nicene churches read it as an early sign of the faith the creeds later set out; Oneness Pentecostals and Unitarians read it differently (see the card).

sections.h: The fellowship of the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 13:14)
sections.b: In the closing blessing, "the fellowship of the Holy Spirit" (2 Corinthians 13:14) can mean the friendship the Spirit makes among believers, or a shared life in the Spirit. In Acts 2:42 the Plain also says "the fellowship". The Spirit is placed beside the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God, as an equal gift to the church.

sections.h: Discipline by witnesses (2 Corinthians 13:1-2, 10)
sections.b: Paul warns that on his third visit he will not spare those who sinned before and did not repent, and quotes the rule of Deuteronomy 19:15: "Every matter will stand on the word of two witnesses or of three" (2 Corinthians 13:1). He wants to use his authority "for building up and not for tearing down" (13:10; compare 10:8). He also says he will wait until the church's own obedience is complete before punishing the rest (10:6). The model is fair hearing, community involvement and restoration as the goal (13:9, 11).
sections.refs: 2 Corinthians 10:6; 2 Corinthians 13:1-2; 2 Corinthians 13:9-11; Deuteronomy 19:15; Matthew 18:16; 1 Corinthians 5:4-5

sections.h: Sexual immorality not repented of (2 Corinthians 12:21)
sections.b: Paul fears that he will mourn over many "who sinned before and have not turned away from the uncleanness, the sexual immorality and the shameless living they practiced" (2 Corinthians 12:21). The three Greek words are akatharsia, porneia and aselgeia. This follows his earlier letter's rebuke over sexual matters at Corinth (1 Corinthians 5; 6:12-20) and shows that some had not changed.

sections.h: The collection and the charge of fraud (2 Corinthians 12:16-18)
sections.b: Some in Corinth said Paul took nothing openly but caught them "with a trick" through the collection (2 Corinthians 12:16). Paul asks whether Titus or the other man he sent made anything off them (12:17-18). The case shows why he insisted that trusted, named men handle the money (2 Corinthians 8:20-21), and how a gift for Jerusalem could be turned into an accusation against its organizer.

sections.h: Titus in 2 Corinthians 12:17-18
sections.b: Paul says he urged Titus to go to Corinth and sent a brother with him, and asks whether Titus took advantage of the Corinthians: "Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not walk in the same footsteps?" (2 Corinthians 12:18). Titus is Paul's trusted envoy to Corinth throughout this letter.

sections.h: Paul and money in Corinth (2 Corinthians 11:7-9; 12:13-14)
sections.b: Paul supported himself and refused to take Corinth's money for preaching, calling it preaching "free of charge" (2 Corinthians 11:7). He took support from the poor churches of Macedonia (11:8-9) and treated his refusal as a mark of his love for the Corinthians (11:11; 12:14-15). The ancient custom was that paid teachers were seen as clients of their patrons; his refusal broke that custom.

sections.h: Testing yourselves (2 Corinthians 13:5)
sections.b: "Check yourselves to see whether you are in the faith. Put yourselves to the test" (2 Corinthians 13:5). Paul uses this to turn back the Corinthians' demand for proof that Christ speaks in him: the proof is Christ in them. Churches have used the verse in different ways for the doctrine of assurance (see the card).

sections.h: Eve and the snake as a warning (2 Corinthians 11:3)
sections.b: Paul uses the story of Genesis 3 for the church: as the snake fooled Eve with his cunning, the Corinthians' thoughts may be led away from simple, pure loyalty to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:3). Eve stands for the church and the snake for whoever deceives it. In Romans 5 the blame falls on Adam; here the point is the danger of being deceived.
